The control ladder

How much help do you actually want?

Hiring a planner isn't all-or-nothing, and it doesn't mean handing over your vision. Pick the level that matches how much you want to keep doing yourself — you can always move up.

Most hands-off

Full Event Planning

For the couple or host with no spare hours

Hand over the whole thing. Your planner builds the concept, sources the venue, books every supplier, manages the budget and runs the day. You approve — you don't chase.

  • Concept, styling direction and mood
  • Venue sourcing and site visits
  • Every supplier sourced, quoted and booked
  • Budget built and tracked for you
  • Run sheet, rehearsal and full day-of management
Full Event Planning
Most popular

Partial Planning

For the planner-at-heart who's run out of runway

You've booked the venue and you have opinions. Your planner picks up the rest — the suppliers you haven't sorted, the timeline, the bits that keep slipping down the list.

  • You keep the decisions you care about
  • Supplier shortlists and introductions
  • Timeline and budget brought back under control
  • Styling refined, not replaced
  • Day-of coordination included
Partial Planning
Keep full control

On-the-Day Coordination

For the host who has it handled — until the day itself

You planned it. Someone else runs it. Your coordinator takes your plan four to six weeks out, confirms every supplier, and is the person everyone calls so nobody calls you.

  • Your plan, your suppliers, your vision
  • Handover four to six weeks out
  • Every supplier confirmed and briefed
  • Run sheet written and distributed
  • On site from bump-in to bump-out

Why people hire a planner

You're not buying a planner. You're buying your headspace back.

Nobody sets out to become the project manager of their own celebration. It happens slowly — one supplier at a time, one spreadsheet tab at a time, until the event you were excited about is a to-do list you're behind on.

A planner takes the list. Not the vision, not the decisions that matter to you — the list.

The supplier who hasn't replied in nine days
The budget spreadsheet that stopped adding up in March
The run sheet nobody else has read
The three group chats you're the admin of
The bump-in time that clashes with the ceremony
The 4pm phone call, on the day, about the chairs

How it works

Four steps, and you're not carrying it any more

01

Tell us what you're planning

One short brief — the occasion, the date, roughly where, and how much help you want. Two minutes, not two hours.

02

We match you to the right planners

Not every planner. The ones who work your occasion, in your area, who are actually free on your date and work at your level of involvement.

Compare quotes and approaches

You'll hear back with pricing, inclusions and how they'd approach your event. Compare in your own time — there's no obligation to book anyone.

04

Hand over the mental load

Choose your planner and stop being the project manager. From here it's their run sheet, their supplier calls, their 4pm problems.

Straight answers

Event planning questions, answered

What does an event planner cost in Australia?
On-the-day coordination typically runs from about $1,200 to $2,500. Partial planning usually sits between $2,500 and $6,000. Full planning is most often quoted at 10–15% of your total event budget, or a flat fee from around $6,000 upwards for a wedding. Pricing moves with guest count, how many suppliers need managing, whether the venue is dry-hire, and how far the planner has to travel. Enquiring through Plan Your Event is free — you only ever pay the planner you choose.
What's the difference between an event planner and an event coordinator?
A planner builds the event: concept, budget, venue, suppliers, timeline — usually starting months or a year out. A coordinator runs an event that's already been planned, taking over four to six weeks before the day to confirm suppliers, write the run sheet and manage the day itself. A stylist is different again — they design and install how it looks, not how it runs. Many planners offer all three as separate packages.
Do I actually need an event planner?
Not always, and a good planner will tell you that. You probably don't need one for a small at-home gathering with two or three suppliers. You probably do if you're managing more than five suppliers, hosting over about 60 guests, using a dry-hire venue, planning from interstate, or if you're one of the key people in the event and can't be answering supplier calls on the day. If you're unsure, on-the-day coordination is the low-commitment place to start.
Will a planner take over my vision?
No — that's the most common worry and it's backwards. A planner's job is to make your decisions happen, not to replace them. You choose how much control you hand over: full planning means they drive and you approve, partial planning means you keep the decisions you care about, and on-the-day coordination means your plan and your suppliers, just executed by someone who isn't you.
How far in advance should I book an event planner?
For a wedding, 9–14 months out is typical, and popular planners book peak Saturdays 12–18 months ahead. For corporate events and milestone parties, 3–6 months is usually enough. On-the-day coordinators can often be booked 2–3 months out, and sometimes later — but availability in October–December and February–April goes first.
Can a planner work with suppliers I've already booked?
Yes. Most events come to a planner half-organised, and that's normal. They'll review what you've booked, flag any gaps or clashes in the timeline, brief your existing suppliers, and only recommend additions where something's genuinely missing. You're not expected to start again.
What happens if something goes wrong on the day?
That's the entire point of having someone on site. Late suppliers, weather calls, a missing delivery, a run sheet that's slipped 25 minutes — your planner or coordinator handles it, usually before you know it happened. Without one, that call comes to you or to a family member in the middle of your own event.
Is it free to enquire through Plan Your Event?
Yes. Sending an enquiry is completely free and there's no obligation to book. You'll receive responses from planners who cover your area and are available on your date, with their pricing and how they'd approach your event, so you can compare properly before committing to anyone.
